newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland presses towards EMU, but Finns unsure.
newsitem.headline: Finland presses towards EMU, but Finns unsure.

text.p: Finland's government on Monday pressed ahead on the road to a single European currency despite clear evidence of popular opposition to the project from voters in European parliament elections.

The day after voters sent some of the country's sharpest Eurosceptics to the Strasbourg-based parliament, the finance ministry briefed journalists on practical preparations in Finland for Economic and Monetary Union in 1999.
"The political drive towards EMU is very, very strong," a senior finance ministry official told reporters.
He said he was referring to Europe in general, but Social Democrat Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen on Sunday underlined Finland's commitment to the planned single currency.
"The EMU train has left and the only alternative for the government is to act as if EMU will take off in 1999," he said.

In a poll with clear echoes of last week's anti-European vote in Austria and last year's roundly negative Swedish vote, the 60 percent of Finns who bothered to vote on Sunday gave strongest support to candidates opposed to further integration.

The two most outspoken EU critics came top: current Euro-MP Paavo Vayrynen, a former foreign minister and the opposition Centre Party's top Eurosceptic, and Esko Seppanen, a rogue anti-European member of the governing Left Wing Alliance.

Analysts said the results, in which the Centre Party grabbed 24.4 percent of the vote against 21.5 percent for the Social Democrats who head the coalition, reflected fears over the single currency not a nationalist protest.

"There was nothing like Austria's populist opposition vote," Pertti Pesonen of Tampere University told Reuters. "Compared with Austria a week ago or Sweden a year ago, the Finns are clearly more satisfied with their European policies."

The vote came 22 months after Finland joined the EU with Austria and Sweden after a referendum which won 57 percent support for membership. Opinion polls before the election had pointed to a broadly unchanged picture until the final days.

Only then did strong support emerge for Eurosceptic candidates capitalising on the government's decision last week to link the Finnish currency, the markka, to Europe's exchange rate mechanism -- a key step towards a single currency.
"It seems that the ERM-link, which we had to do, has had an effect," said Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto on Sunday.

Around 60 percent of Finns have said they oppose a single currency, but Lipponen's government says it has no choice but to get the country in shape for EMU so that when the time comes, it does not risk being left out.
"The Finns want a place at the top table in Europe," one western diplomat said.

But analysts said the vote could fuel pressure on the government to hold a referendum on joining EMU. Polls in neighbouring Sweden on Sunday showed a majority of Swedes -- who are broadly more negative about EU membership -- want one.
